Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation — Product Metrics & Measurement

Metric Definitions and Data Quality

Why two dashboards disagree, who owns the sentence that settles it, and what it costs when nobody does.

1. Two decisions, one week apart

On 11 August 2026, Devika Rane, vice-president of product at Arka Mobility, a Pune-based electric two-wheeler ride-hailing and rental marketplace, was looking at a number she had approved four months earlier. Arka's quarterly rider-incentive budget of ₹9.4 crore was allocated city by city on weekly active riders, a metric she had changed in April at the growth team's request: stitch a rider's sessions across a 60-minute idle gap rather than 30, and count a rider as active on any session rather than only on a completed ride.

The change had done something else as well. Weekly active riders in Pune rose 11.4 percent the week it shipped. Nagpur, where a thinner fleet produced longer gaps between app opens, gained 19.2 percent from the same edit. Neither city had grown. Roughly ₹1.7 crore of incentive spend had been reallocated by a session-stitching parameter. Devika had until the 21st, when the operating review convened, to say whether the April definition should stand, and whether two quarters of reporting built on it should be restated.

In Hyderabad, on 18 August, Aparna Iyer, director of product at Bhavantar Health Cloud, faced the same problem with a sharper edge. Bhavantar sells claims-adjudication software to health insurers and third-party administrators, and its agreements with nine customers carry a commitment on clean claim rate — the share of claims passing adjudication without manual intervention — with a floor of 92 percent and service credits payable below it. Bhavantar's dashboard reported 94.1 percent for the June quarter; a customer's audit team, computing the same metric from records exported through Bhavantar's own API, reported 88.6 percent.

The gap was entirely definitional. Bhavantar counted each claim once, at final disposition; the customer counted each submission, so a claim rejected for a missing document and resubmitted successfully counted twice, once dirty and once clean. Both were correct. Across nine contracts the exposure was roughly ₹4.2 crore, and October's renewal would open from a position of having, in the customer's words, reported against a definition chosen after the fact. Aparna's problem was not to win the argument but to work out which definition Bhavantar should have been able to point to before the quarter began.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A metric definition is a written, versioned specification fixing six things: the source records that feed the number; the population eligible to be counted; the predicate qualifying a member of that population as counted; the window, with timezone and boundary convention; the identity rule resolving raw rows into countable units; and the restatement policy for when history changes underneath it. Data quality is the orthogonal question of whether those records are complete, timely, accurate and stable. The two are constantly confused, and expensively, because the remedies point in opposite directions: a definitional disagreement is repaired by a sentence two people sign, a data-quality defect by engineering.

Three traditions converge here and have never merged. Accounting met the problem two centuries before software and solved it institutionally — a standards body (in India, the ICAI with Ind AS), an audit, disclosed policies, a restatement procedure — its insight being that a definition's authority comes from process, not correctness. Measurement theory, from psychometrics, contributes construct validity and the vocabulary of bias and measurement error, treating a metric as an estimator rather than a fact. The business-intelligence lineage contributes the semantic layer — define once, reuse everywhere — from 1990s BI universes through LookML to dbt's metric models, later paired with observability tooling that put freshness and schema drift under service-level objectives.

Alongside all three runs Goodhart's 1975 observation, in a form specific to this topic: it is not only the measured behaviour that adapts to the target but the definition, because whoever can edit it is usually whoever is evaluated by it. Devika's session-stitch change is the canonical instance. Four schools argue about what follows.

The certification school holds that a company should keep a small number of governed definitions in code, each with an owner and change control. It signs: no number reaches a board pack, a contract or a compensation plan unless it resolves to a certified definition. It will not sign that teams may publish local variants for their own decisions. The federated school, from data-mesh thinking, holds that definitions belong to the domain teams who understand the process, and that the centre owns interoperability — discoverability, versioning, producer-consumer contracts — not adjudication. It signs: every definition must be discoverable, versioned and contracted with its consumers; it will not sign that a central council should approve every change.

The decision-first school holds that a definition earns maintenance only where a named decision changes when the number moves. It signs: no metric without an owner, a decision and a review cadence; it will not sign that a catalog of four hundred certified metrics helps anyone. The measurement-error school holds that a single certified number is a fiction. It signs: a published value is incomplete without an as-of date and a maturity lag; it will not sign that one definition can be declared correct, since correctness belongs to an estimator relative to a construct, not to SQL.

These do not reconcile by synthesis, and pretending otherwise is how governance programmes fail. Adopt certification wholesale and within eighteen months you hold a catalog the decision-first school calls waste. Adopt federation wholesale and, the day a contract is disputed, you stand where Bhavantar stands: two defensible definitions and no adjudicator.

3. Mechanics: the estimator, the lag and the elasticity

Expert practice treats a reported metric as an estimator of a quantity the business cares about. Write the reported value as the true quantity plus named distortions: M = T + I + L + D, where I is instrumentation bias (events not sent, or sent twice), L the late-arrival deficit, and D identity distortion (one human counted as three devices, or three humans as one account). Each has a different owner, and conflating them is the commonest technical error here.

Late arrival comes first, because it is most often mistaken for real movement. Arka's app buffers session events when a rider loses coverage and flushes them on reconnection. Devika's team re-read one reporting day at successive as-of dates: 1,148,000 sessions at D+0, then 1,281,000, 1,318,000 and 1,329,000 on the three following days, settling at 1,333,000 by D+7. The live dashboard was showing 86.1 percent of the final figure. The quantity that matters is the maturity lag — days until the value reaches 99 percent of its final level, here two. Any comparison placing a mature day beside a fresh one manufactures a fourteen-percent decline every morning. The fix is to publish the metric with its as-of date and refuse to render immature days in the same series as mature ones.

The identity term is larger and quieter. Arka's ratio of device identifiers to logged-in rider identifiers was 1.31 in June. When marketing ran a campaign deep-linking into the app without forcing a login, it reached 1.44 in three weeks. Rider behaviour had not changed; the share of sessions resolvable to a known rider had fallen, and unresolved sessions counted as new devices. Any device-level identity rule inflates whenever the login rate falls — which means a metric can be moved by a change to a signup screen that nobody mentioned to the analytics team. The expert response is to instrument the resolution rate as a first-class series beside the metric, and to attach service-level objectives to the metric rather than the source table, since a freshness alert tells an engineer a pipeline is late but does not tell Devika whether the number is safe to present on Thursday.

The formal step most often skipped is definitional elasticity — the sensitivity of the number to each parameter, computed deliberately rather than discovered by accident. After August, Arka recomputed six weeks of history across a parameter grid.

Session-stitch idle gapPredicate: any sessionPredicate: completed ride
15 minutes2,461,0001,702,000
30 minutes (definition v1)2,288,0001,698,000
60 minutes (definition v2)2,043,0001,691,000
120 minutes1,897,0001,684,000

Two second-order findings follow. The session predicate has an elasticity to the stitching constant of about minus twenty-three percent across the plausible range; the ride predicate, about one percent. A metric swinging by a quarter on an arbitrary engineering constant is poor not because the constant is wrong but because its variance across defensible parameter choices exceeds the effect anyone is trying to detect. Devika's real finding was that the whole session-based family was unusable for allocating budget.

And v2 yields a lower count than v1, since a longer stitch merges sessions — yet Pune rose 11.4 percent when v2 shipped. That contradiction is the tell that something else moved too, and it had: the predicate changed from completed ride to any session in the same pull request. Bundling two definitional changes into one release destroys the ability to attribute a step to either, which is why serious teams dual-run and publish the expected step before cutover.

4. When the discipline pays, and when it misleads

The conditions under which formal definitions repay their cost are testable claims. One: more than one team computes the number independently. True at Arka, where growth, city operations and finance each kept a rider count; true at Bhavantar in the worst form, the second team being a customer. Two: money moves with the number — ₹9.4 crore of allocation at Arka, ₹4.2 crore of contingent credits at Bhavantar. Where money moves with a number, its definition is a contract term whether or not anyone wrote it as one. Three: the countable unit has contested identity — device, login or household at Arka; claim or submission at Bhavantar. Four: the data is mutable after the fact. True at both.

Where the claims fail, the discipline becomes overhead and then the frozen wrong definition. A seed-stage company with one analyst gains nothing from change control and loses the ability to improve its measurement weekly, which at that stage beats comparability. It is actively misleading in three further cases: where a metric's value lies in direction rather than level, formalising the level invites precision theatre; where a construct has no single correct operationalisation — engagement for a content product — certifying one variant suppresses a disagreement rather than settling it; and where governance runs slower than the learning cycle, teams route around it, which breeds shadow metrics and killed the programme in section eight.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Multi-product companies hit the union problem. A group-level active-user count is the union of the products, requiring a cross-product identity graph most firms lack, or the sum, which double-counts, or the largest product alone, honest but uninformative. Cheeni Foods, a Mumbai direct-to-consumer staples brand with a subscription line and a marketplace storefront, found its group figure ran 8 percent above the true union because one subscriber in twelve also bought through the storefront under a different email. The mature answer is not to fix the identity graph but to publish the sum with a measured overlap adjustment, labelled as such.

Two-sided marketplaces face the same word meaning different things on each side. Bageecha, a Bengaluru plants-and-garden marketplace, calls a seller active on a live listing, which flatters supply, and a buyer active on a completed order, which is strict. The asymmetry is not accidental: each side's metric was written by the team recruiting that side. Gross merchandise value compounds it, since conventions on refunds and platform discounts move the figure fifteen to twenty percent and every incentive points to the generous one.

Regulated contexts invert ownership. Chirantan General Insurance reports a claim settlement ratio to the IRDAI under a statutory definition, while its claims and product teams need one that excludes claims still inside their permitted assessment window, since the statutory figure penalises a claim merely for being young. Mature firms keep both, declare the statutory one authoritative externally, and publish a permanent reconciliation bridge. The bridge is the artifact; the identity is the fiction.

Hardware plus software is harder than either. Chakori Devices, a Coimbatore maker of connected water purifiers with a companion app, found that a May firmware release had changed the semantics of its core usage event: what had fired per dispensing cycle began firing per session at the tap. Litres per household appeared to fall 27 percent across the auto-updated base while the rest stayed flat. Part of the definition lived in firmware, which ships on its own schedule to an unevenly upgraded fleet and cannot be corrected in the field. Chakori versioned the event schema in the payload and computed the metric per firmware cohort, making the discontinuity visible rather than silently averaged.

AI-native products bring a distinctive variant. Anuvaad AI, a Gurugram company whose product drafts support replies in eleven Indian languages, reports suggestion acceptance rate as its quality metric. Three things move it without touching quality: a UI change that pre-selects the top suggestion, a retry policy that counts two suggestions where there was one, and — the novel one — a model upgrade that shifts the distribution of what is suggested. A model version change is a silent redefinition performed by an artifact rather than a person, so the usual control, a human signature, never fires. Anuvaad made model version a mandatory dimension and refused to draw a line across a version boundary without dual-running the old model on a holdout slice.

At the organisational seams, practice differs from the data-strategy deck. The deck says one source of truth. Firms that have survived a few disputes run two tiers: a small certified tier of fifteen to twenty-five metrics, versioned and dual-run on change; and a large uncertified tier anyone may create, labelled uncertified wherever it is rendered. The value sits in the labelling, not the catalog. They also keep permanent bridges between the product-side and finance-side versions of the metrics that matter, making the gap a monitored quantity rather than a recurring argument.

6. Eight things experts see that competent practitioners miss

The disagreement is almost never the pipeline. A strong engineer's instinct is to audit the pipeline; an expert's is to look at the shape of the gap over time. A stable ratio — 2.6× every month for nine months — is the signature of a population or predicate difference, because a data defect produces an erratic gap. The obvious reading, that a surprising number means broken data, costs three weeks on instrumentation when the fix was a sentence.

A metric is a function of as-of date, not a value. The tell is someone screenshotting a dashboard to lock a number for a deck: the act admits the number will change. The obvious reading, that the dashboard is unreliable, is wrong — it is faithfully disclosing late-arriving data. What is missing is a published maturity lag and a convention about which as-of date each audience gets.

Identity resolution is the largest lever nobody watches. The tell is a device-to-user ratio drifting after an unrelated product change, as at Arka. Experts instrument the resolution rate and treat a move in it as an incident. The obvious reading treats identity as an engineering detail; in fact it determines what the unit of the metric is, and a metric with an unstable unit has no interpretable history.

Definitions are incentives, so write them to be read adversarially. The tell is an exclusion list that always removes the unflattering rows: test accounts, refunded orders, voucher-funded transactions, claims still in assessment. Each exclusion is individually defensible; the pattern is the finding. The obvious reading argues each rule on its merits. An expert asks who benefits from the accumulated set, and whether that person can edit it.

Versioning without a restatement policy is half a system. The tell is a changelog beside charts that silently splice v1 history to v2 present. Three policies are defensible — restate, break the series visibly at the change date, or dual-run for a stated period — and the failure is not picking the wrong one but having none, which leaves the choice to whoever writes the next query.

The value of a metrics catalog falls as it grows. The tell is a hundred-plus certified entries in a company where analysts still write their own SQL. Certification is a scarce signal: it says this number has been fought over and someone will answer for it. Applied to everything it says nothing, and search costs rise until the catalog is worse than asking a colleague. The obvious reading mistakes an index for a guarantee.

Quality objectives belong to metrics, not tables. The tell is a tool alerting on table freshness while nobody can say whether tomorrow's board number is safe. Table monitoring is necessary and insufficient: it has no notion of which business question degrades when a column goes stale. Experts publish, per certified metric, the dependencies, the tolerated revision and the person paged.

Definition changes need a null-change test, and an owner who can refuse. The tell is a team shipping a redefinition and interpreting the step the same week; expert practice publishes the expected step before cutover, so an unexplained residual becomes a finding rather than noise absorbed into a growth narrative. The companion tell is an owner who cannot account for a six-percent move within a day. What cannot be delegated is the authority to decline a change and the duty to explain movements.

7. How this changes across product types and stages

In consumer products the difficulty is identity and the weakness of activity as evidence of value, which is why consumer companies migrate their headline metric from opens toward transactions. In B2B and enterprise software the unit becomes account and seat, and the hard question is aggregation: does one active seat make a thousand-seat account active? Because enterprise counts are small, one misclassified account visibly moves a rate, so errors are more embarrassing and far easier to detect. Enterprise adds a feature no other type has: the definition may be a contract term, with a customer's audit team on the other side.

For platforms and marketplaces the distinctive issue is two populations with asymmetric definitions and a value metric whose conventions are unusually elastic. For hardware, part of the definition ships in firmware and cannot be backfilled. For AI products, the model is a definitional dependency that changes without human sign-off. Beyond those specifics the mechanics are identical, and most of what is written about B2B versus consumer metrics here is not a real difference: the six clauses, the revision profile and the ownership question do not vary.

Stage matters more than type. At seed the definition lives in one analyst's head, which is correct: formality costs more than divergence, and the real risk is that the analyst leaves. At Series B and C, where Arka sits, two or three teams start computing independently and money begins moving with numbers; this is when the six clauses must be written down, and when most companies do not, because nothing has yet gone visibly wrong. At scale the constraint inverts: definitions couple to hundreds of dashboards, compensation plans and contracts, so the dominant cost is no longer divergence but change, and the programmes that work make change cheap and visible rather than rare.

8. Three worked examples

Cheeni Foods and the repeat-rate denominator. Growth reported a 41 percent ninety-day repeat rate; finance reported 29 percent. Both counted the same numerator. The denominator differed: growth used first-order customers in the cohort month who had not requested a refund, while finance used all first-time purchasers, including the 6 percent who returned their first order, and included a quick-commerce listing where repeat purchase was unobservable and therefore counted as zero. Removing the unobservable channel from both parts of the fraction, and agreeing to include refunded first orders, produced 34 percent, which both teams signed. The reconciled figure did not sit between the two: one adjustment raised it, the other lowered it — the intuition that truth lies between two estimates fails when adjustments act on different parts of a ratio.

Bhavantar and the contractual denominator. Aparna's team recomputed the June quarter under both readings: 94.1 percent claim-level, 88.6 percent submission-level. A third reading — claim-level, excluding claims where manual intervention followed the insurer's own missing pre-authorisation — gave 96.3 percent, and was the figure the sales team used in pitches: the most generous of the three, and written into no contract. Aparna recommended conceding the submission-level reading for the disputed quarter, an estimated ₹1.1 crore after negotiation, and amending every agreement at renewal with a defined denominator, a stated exclusion list, a monthly window and a jointly readable reconciliation. The concession bought the right to write the clause.

Ambar Stays, where the approach failed. Ambar, a Jaipur homestay booking platform, ran a certification programme through 2025: a council certified 240 metrics in eleven months, required approval for any change and mandated that all reporting use the certified layer. Fourteen months in, an audit found 31 percent of active dashboards queried that layer; the rest sat on raw tables. Median time from change request to approval was 23 days, against a two-week release cadence. The tooling worked. The programme failed because governance latency exceeded the learning cycle, making evasion rational for any team under delivery pressure, and because certifying 240 metrics destroyed the signal value of certification. Recovery took two quarters: the certified tier was cut to nineteen, everything else relabelled uncertified rather than deleted, approval moved to a named owner per metric with a two-day service level, and dual-running became mandatory. Certified-layer use for board and compensation reporting reached 100 percent because the rule was narrowed to those two uses; elsewhere the label did the work.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Silent redefinition. Early sign: a step change with no product or market event on the same date. Diagnostic: what changed in the code computing this metric in the two weeks before the step? Cost of catching it late: at Arka, ₹1.7 crore of allocation distributed on a distortion rather than on performance, plus a growth narrative that now needs correcting.

Maturity confusion. Early sign: a recurring dip that always affects the most recent day. Diagnostic: what is the maturity lag, and is the chart mixing as-of dates? Cost of catching it late: decisions taken on a phantom decline, and a company that learns to ignore recent data.

Ownership diffusion. Early sign: when the number is challenged, three people give different accounts and nobody names an approver. Diagnostic: who signs off a change, and can the room name them in ten seconds? Cost of catching it late: drift by accumulated local fixes until no version matches any description.

Exclusion creep. Early sign: the exclusion list has grown by a rule a quarter and every rule improved the number. Diagnostic: what would this read with all discretionary exclusions removed? Cost of catching it late: an auditor, acquirer or customer finds it first, and the company argues about its integrity rather than its arithmetic.

Governance latency. Early sign: the share of reporting on the governed layer falls while the catalog grows. Diagnostic: median days-to-approval, against the release cadence? Cost of catching it late: Ambar's outcome — a platform 69 percent of the company routed around, and two quarters spent dismantling it.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Central certification versus federated ownership. The certification case rests on the observation that every documented metrics disaster involves two teams computing independently, and that contracts, compensation and board reporting need one adjudicable answer. It would be wrong if governance latency reliably exceeded the learning cycle, which Ambar suggests is common. The federated case rests on domain teams holding the process knowledge and councils becoming bottlenecks, with adoption figures like Ambar's as evidence. It would be wrong if contracts and discoverability proved insufficient without an adjudicator — which is what happens the day a customer disputes a number.

Should the board metric equal the operating metric? One camp holds that a company reporting one number externally while managing by another is lying to someone. The other holds that external reporting optimises for comparability while operating metrics optimise for sensitivity, and that forcing identity degrades both — insurance being the clearest case, where the regulator's definition is authoritative and internally unusable. The first is wrong if a published bridge reliably stops divergence becoming deception; the second, if dual numbers always drift toward the convenient one.

Is data quality an engineering objective or a product judgement? The engineering position treats quality as availability, with objectives, alerting and error budgets; it is wrong if the worst failures are definitional, since no freshness monitor catches a correctly computed wrong construct. The product position treats quality as validity — is this measuring what we think? — and is wrong if most incidents really are pipeline failures, which at some companies they demonstrably are. The mix differs by company, and few firms have measured their own.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in three visible ways. Hearing two conflicting numbers, they ask for the shape of the gap over time before asking anyone to check the pipeline, and they want the two definitions in one sentence each rather than the two queries. They treat every number they present as carrying an as-of date and a version, and say so aloud. And they are stingy with certification: they keep the governed list under twenty, decline to certify a metric whose owning decision cannot be named, and dual-run before a change rather than after — because this discipline is paid for at a predictable time in advance, and skipping it is paid for at the worst possible time, in front of someone who matters.

12. What each protagonist decided

On 21 August, Devika Rane proposed that weekly active riders be retired as an allocation basis in favour of riders with at least one completed ride in the week — a predicate with an elasticity of one percent to the stitching constant rather than twenty-three. She did not propose restating two quarters of history; she proposed breaking the series visibly at the April date, publishing both definitions for the overlap, and rebalancing the September-quarter allocation on the new basis, which moved ₹62 lakh from Nagpur to Pune and Nashik. Restatement's cost was arguing about the past; the allocation's cost was still misdirecting money, and only one of those lay in the future.

On 27 August, Aparna Iyer recommended that Bhavantar concede the submission-level reading and negotiate credits rather than litigate the definition, on the argument that a vendor who argues about the denominator after the fact loses the renewal even when it wins the quarter. The structural recommendation mattered more: a defined denominator and exclusion list in every renewed agreement, monthly measurement, a jointly readable reconciliation, and a rule that no number shipped to a customer may come from a definition that customer cannot reproduce from the data Bhavantar exports.

Three questions for discussion. First, Devika chose to break the series rather than restate it: under what conditions would restatement have been better, and what would she have to believe about how Arka's board reads history? Second, Bhavantar's most generous reading, 96.3 percent, was used in pitches and written into nothing — governance failure, sales failure, or the predictable result of letting an uncertified metric into customer-facing material? Third, if you had to cut your own certified list to nineteen entries tomorrow, which would survive, and what does the part you cannot bring yourself to cut say about which decisions are actually made from numbers?

13. Going deeper

  1. Designing an event taxonomy — definitions sit on top of it; an ambiguous event name guarantees an ambiguous metric, and no governance layer repairs it downstream.
  2. Self-serve analytics and metric layers — one governed definition exposed to many non-analysts, which makes a certified tier operational rather than aspirational.
  3. What makes a good metric — sensitivity, stability and diagnosticity, which explain why Arka's session predicate failed as an estimator.
  4. Vanity vs actionable metrics — a metric with no named decision behind it drifts, because nobody notices when it stops being true.
  5. GAME framework — goals to actions to metrics to evaluation, a way to decide what deserves certification.
  6. Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions — the families where denominators are most often silently inconsistent, as Cheeni Foods found.
  7. Direct vs proxy, magnitude vs ratio — counting the thing versus counting a correlate, where most elasticity enters a metrics tree.
  8. North Star metric — the highest-stakes definitional choice a company makes, and where Goodhart's adaptation of the definition is likeliest.

Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation — Product Metrics & Measurement

Metric Definitions and Data Quality

1. A number for the board that nobody could defend

On the morning of 9 September 2026, Meera Krishnan, head of product analytics at Rasoi Express, a Bengaluru grocery-delivery company preparing a Series C round, pulled up two slides for the same board pack. The marketing dashboard, built off an event stream from the mobile app, showed monthly active users climbing from 713,000 in July to 842,000 in August — an 18 percent jump the CEO had already started rehearsing as the headline number for investors. The finance dashboard, built independently by the revenue-operations team off the order-management database, showed active customers rising from 302,000 to 316,000 — a 4.6 percent increase. Both dashboards were labelled "MAU." Both were, in a narrow technical sense, correct.

The stakes were not abstract. Rasoi Express was in diligence with two growth-stage funds, and the model an investor builds off a claimed 18 percent monthly growth rate looks very different from one built off 4.6 percent. If the marketing number stood unchallenged and a due-diligence analyst later pulled the raw order data, the company would look careless or, worse, deliberately generous with its own metrics. If Meera killed the number without a clear account of the disagreement, she would hand the CEO a credibility problem two weeks before a term sheet was due. She had four days to produce a number she could defend under cross-examination.

2. The idea: a metric is not a number until someone owns it

A metric definition is a written, versioned specification of exactly what a number counts: which raw events or records feed it, which population it is drawn from, what is excluded, over what time window, in which timezone, and who is accountable for changing it. The discipline of writing these down deliberately — rather than letting each analyst infer them from a shared table — is sometimes called metrics governance, and the artifact itself is often called a metric contract. Data quality is a related but separate idea: it is whether the underlying data feeding a definition is complete, timely, and accurate, regardless of how well the definition itself is written. The Rasoi Express board slide had a data quality problem in neither dashboard; both pipelines were accurate against their own definitions. It had a definitions problem: two people had answered the question "what counts as an active user?" differently, and neither had written the answer down anywhere the other could see.

The problem is old, but its modern vocabulary hardened over roughly two periods. In the late 2000s, growth teams at consumer internet companies popularised "daily active users" and "monthly active users" as standard health metrics, then discovered that different teams inside the same company computed them differently — some counting app opens, some sessions, some any server request. Analytics vendors of that era shipped their own defaults, which rarely matched a company's internal definition, compounding the confusion. A second wave, roughly 2019 to 2022, came from the "semantic layer" or "metrics layer" in tools such as dbt and LookML, which let a company define a metric once, in code, so every dashboard queries that single definition rather than reimplementing it. The single sentence Meera could say in the boardroom without sounding glib is this: a metric is not a number until it has an owner, a written definition, and a version number that changes every time the definition does.

3. How it actually works: from raw event to reportable number

Building a defensible metric definition means making choices explicit that most teams leave implicit until a disagreement forces the issue. The first is the source: which raw table or event stream feeds the number. Marketing at Rasoi Express used the app's app_opened event, logged whenever the app came to the foreground, including background refreshes on some Android devices. Finance used order_completed rows from the transactional database, which fire only when payment clears.

The second is population: who is eligible to be counted at all. Marketing counted any device ID that had ever opened the app, including QA test devices and a large batch of dormant accounts from a defunct 2024 loyalty-card promotion. Finance counted only customer IDs tied to a completed KYC record, which excluded guest checkouts.

The third is the activity threshold: what counts as "active." Marketing's threshold was one app open; finance's was one completed, paid order. These are not close substitutes — at Rasoi Express roughly one in three app opens in a given month never converts to an order.

The fourth is the time window and its edges: calendar month versus trailing 30 days. Rasoi Express operates entirely in IST, so timezone was not the fault line, but the window convention still differed: marketing used calendar month, finance a trailing 30-day window ending on the reporting date, which shifts against calendar boundaries and quietly changes which orders fall inside the count near month-end.

The step practitioners most often skip is the fifth: writing all four choices down in one place, attaching an owner's name, and versioning the specification so it changes visibly whenever any input does. Without that document, two competent analysts will independently make reasonable-sounding choices and arrive at numbers that differ by a factor of two and a half, exactly as happened here.

4. A worked reconciliation, line by line

Meera's first task was not to pick a winner but to build a bridge table that explained the gap arithmetically. She started from the marketing figure of 842,000 app-opening devices in August. Of those, roughly 1.9 percent, or 16,000, were QA and internal test devices that never belonged in the denominator, bringing the figure to 826,000. A further 9 percent, about 74,000, were devices tied to the 2024 loyalty-card promotion that had never completed KYC and were structurally ineligible to transact — down to 752,000. Of that remainder, Rasoi Express's own funnel data showed that 58 percent of monthly app-opening, KYC-eligible devices placed no order in the period, which removes 436,000 and leaves 316,000 — matching finance's figure almost exactly, since its trailing-30-day window covers nearly the same span as marketing's calendar month. Laid out as a table, the reconciliation looked like this.

Adjustment stepUsers remaining
Marketing MAU (app opens, calendar month, all devices)842,000
Less: QA / internal test devices826,000
Less: non-KYC devices (2024 promotion cohort)752,000
Less: KYC devices with zero completed orders in period316,000
Finance MAU (completed orders, trailing 30 days, KYC only)316,000

The exercise mattered less for the final number than for what it proved: the dashboards were not disagreeing about data quality — every step reconciled cleanly — they were disagreeing about population and threshold choices never written down together. Meera then tested how sensitive the finance number was to one further choice: whether to count orders placed with a first-time-user discount voucher, which revenue operations had historically excluded as not "real" revenue. Including them raised August's paying-customer count from 316,000 to 351,000, an 11 percent jump driven entirely by a definitional switch — larger than the 4.6 percent underlying growth the business had actually produced. That exclusion rule, buried in one analyst's personal script with no documentation, could move the headline number more than the business itself had moved.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

Cadence is not interchangeable

Daily, weekly, and monthly active-user counts capture different behaviour patterns, not the same metric at different intervals; a product with strong weekly engagement but weak daily engagement looks healthy on one and mediocre on the other. Choosing a cadence is choosing what kind of habit to observe.

Numerator and denominator must be defined together

A rate like "activation rate" is meaningless until both the numerator (what counts as activated) and the denominator (out of whom — signups, installs, or KYC-completed accounts) are fixed. Teams often argue about the numerator while quietly using different denominators.

A metric divorced from a decision becomes vanity

The test of whether a definition is worth maintaining is whether some named decision changes when the number moves. If no one can say what decision MAU informs, the definition will drift unnoticed.

Data quality and definition disagreement are different failure modes

A number can be wrong because a pipeline dropped rows, arrived late, or double-counted — a data-quality failure — or because it faithfully computes an outdated or ambiguous definition. Treating the second as the first sends teams to "fix the pipeline" when the fix is to fix the specification.

Backfills silently rewrite history

When a delayed event stream catches up, or a source table is corrected retroactively, historical metric values can shift after the fact. A dashboard showing a different value for last month than it showed a week ago is not necessarily broken; it may simply be disclosing late-arriving data.

Version debt accumulates invisibly

When a definition changes, old dashboards and saved reports keep referencing the previous version unless the change is actively broadcast. Without a version number and changelog, "MAU" quietly becomes several different numbers wearing one label.

Ownership diffused across teams is ownership held by no one

A metric that "everyone" is responsible for tends to have no one who can explain a sudden move in it. Clear ownership does not mean one person computes the number; it means one person is accountable for the definition and must approve any change to it.

A correct definition still cannot tell you why a number moved

Even a perfectly specified, well-governed metric answers only "what happened," never "why." Rasoi Express could define MAU with total rigor and still need separate diagnostic work — cohort analysis, qualitative research — to explain a 4.6 percent move.

6. How this differs by business type and company stage

In consumer products like Rasoi Express, the central tension is device-level identity: one device may serve a household, and app-open events are cheap to generate but weak evidence of intent, which is why consumer companies migrate their primary metric from activity toward value, such as a completed transaction. In B2B products, the unit shifts from device or person to account and seat: "active accounts" must specify whether one active seat makes a whole enterprise account active, and because B2B counts are often in the hundreds, one misclassified account can swing the reported rate visibly. In marketplace products, definitions must serve two populations, supply and demand, and a metric like gross merchandise value must state whether it is gross or net of refunds and platform discounts, since marketplaces have every incentive to prefer whichever convention flatters growth. Company stage matters as much as business type: an early-stage company typically has one analyst who holds the definition in their head and reproduces it by habit, which works until that person leaves; a company at Rasoi Express's stage needs it written down because two teams are now building independently; and a large company typically builds a metrics catalog or semantic layer with a governance council, because the cost of an ungoverned redefinition scales with how many dashboards and compensation plans quietly depend on the old number.

7. Common mistakes

Parallel pipelines from one source table. Symptom: two dashboards claiming to show the same metric disagree by a wide margin with no obvious data-quality issue in either. Misunderstanding: teams assume querying the same raw table guarantees the same answer, when the filtering logic layered on top actually determines the number. Cheapest diagnostic: pull both SQL queries side by side and diff the WHERE and JOIN clauses before touching either team's data.

Silent redefinition. Symptom: a historical trend line shows an unexplained step change with no corresponding product or market event. Misunderstanding: someone changed a filter to fix a local problem without recording it as a new version. Cheapest diagnostic: check the change history of the query or model that computes the metric around that date.

No named owner. Symptom: when the number is questioned in a meeting, three people explain it slightly differently and none can say who would approve a change to it. Misunderstanding: ownership was assumed implicit in whichever team built the first dashboard. Cheapest diagnostic: ask directly who signs off if the definition changes, and see whether the room agrees on one name within ten seconds.

Treating a definitions problem as a data-quality problem. Symptom: a number looks too low, and the team's first instinct is to audit the pipeline for missing rows. Misunderstanding: assuming any surprising number reflects broken data rather than a narrow or stale definition. Cheapest diagnostic: before touching the pipeline, restate the definition in one sentence and ask a colleague from another team whether they would write the same sentence.

8. What good looks like

Six weeks after the board meeting, Rasoi Express had a metrics registry named Manak, a single internal document set where every reportable metric had one page: its name, its owner, its exact SQL logic, its version history, the decision it was meant to inform, and its review cadence. "Monthly active customers" now had one definition — a KYC-verified customer who completed at least one paid order in the calendar month — owned jointly by Meera and the head of revenue operations, who had to co-sign any proposed change before it shipped. Both the marketing and finance dashboards now queried the same underlying view rather than reimplementing the logic separately, so a change to the definition propagated to every downstream report automatically instead of requiring someone to remember which dashboards needed updating. When a new analyst proposed excluding voucher-funded orders again, the change went through a two-day review against the registry rather than a quiet edit to a personal script, and the registry entry recorded exactly why the exclusion was rejected this time, so the same argument would not have to be relitigated at the next board cycle.

9. What Meera decided, and what to learn next

Meera presented the board with neither number alone. She showed the bridge table, labelled the two definitions explicitly, and proposed a single primary growth metric going forward — calendar-month KYC-verified paying customers — while noting that app engagement, tracked separately, remained a useful but secondary signal of interest that had not yet converted to revenue. The board's reaction was calmer than she expected: investors who had seen inflated growth stories before were reassured precisely because the company could explain its own arithmetic, and the 4.6 percent figure, defended rigorously, did more for Rasoi Express's credibility than the unexamined 18 percent figure would have done if it survived first contact with due diligence.

Having settled how one metric is defined and governed, the natural next step is to ask how many people can safely be given the ability to query it without recreating the same divergence — which is the province of self-serve analytics and metric layers, where a single governed definition is exposed to non-analysts through a shared semantic layer rather than reimplemented ad hoc in every new dashboard. Two questions worth sitting with: when your own dashboards disagree, is the disagreement about data quality or about an unwritten definitional choice, and can you name, right now, the one person who would need to approve a change to the metric your team reports most often?

Karmik: The Night Before the Reconciliation

A staffing marketplace has four numbers for how many workers it has, three sources for whether a shift happened, a ₹6.8 crore client dispute, and eight days.

1. Sunday night, Indiranagar

On Sunday, 8 February 2026, a little after eleven at night, Ira Kothari sat at her dining table in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with three printouts in front of her and a fourth she had deliberately not printed. She was Karmik's chief product officer, and by Monday evening she was expected to bring a recommendation to the founders on what Karmik would say, in writing, to its largest customer by 14 February.

The first printout was the notice. On 15 January, Tvarit Retail — a quick-commerce operator running 340 dark stores across nine cities, and Karmik's single largest account — had written disputing ₹6.82 crore of invoices covering April 2025 to January 2026, on the grounds that Karmik had billed for shifts its store managers said had not been worked. The contract gave Karmik thirty days to respond and gave Tvarit an audit right and a ninety-day termination clause.

The second printout was a one-page memo from Karmik's head of data science in Toronto, dated 20 January, which concluded that Karmik's headline figure of 1.1 lakh monthly active workers — the number in every investor conversation since November — should properly be about 74,000.

The third printout was the auditors' cut-off query, raised on 2 February, asking Karmik to demonstrate the basis on which revenue on shift-based billing was recognised. The fourth document, the one she had not printed, was a two-line message from Karmik's customer-success lead in Singapore saying that Zubara Facilities Management in Dubai had asked, "informally for now", for the same kind of reconciliation.

Ira had spent nine days trying to establish a simple thing: how many shifts had actually been worked. She had not managed it. What she had established was that Karmik possessed at least three systems that believed they knew, that each had been right at some point in the company's history, and that the question of which one was authoritative had never been decided by anybody.

2. How Karmik got here

Karmik Staffing Technologies was founded in Bengaluru in 2018 by Rajat Sinha, a former operations manager at a logistics firm, and Deepa Kamat, an engineer. It matched frontline workers — warehouse pickers, delivery riders, retail promoters, facility staff, quick-service restaurant crew — with employers who needed them by the shift rather than by the year. Workers registered on a mobile app available in Hindi, Kannada, Telugu, Bengali and Tamil; employers posted shift requirements; Karmik sourced, verified, deployed, tracked attendance, disbursed wages and handled EPFO and ESIC compliance. It billed employers a rate per shift that included the worker's wage, statutory contributions, and Karmik's markup of about thirteen per cent, plus a platform fee for its workforce-management software. In the year to March 2026 it expected gross billings of about ₹1,240 crore, net revenue of ₹158 crore and an EBITDA loss of ₹22 crore.

Two decisions from its early years constrained everything Ira could now do. The first was made in 2020. Karmik chose to identify workers by mobile number rather than by a government identifier, partly because the founders judged that asking for Aadhaar at registration would suppress sign-ups among the migrant workers who were its core supply, and partly on legal advice about handling identifiers, advice that the DPDP Act later reinforced. The consequence was that a worker who changed numbers — common among migrant workers moving between Bengaluru, Hyderabad and their home districts — became a new worker. Nobody knew how many duplicates the system contained.

The second was made in 2021, when Karmik won its first large third-party logistics contract. To close the deal, Karmik agreed that attendance, and therefore billing, would be evidenced by punches recorded in Karmik's own worker app. That clause was copied into every enterprise contract thereafter, including Tvarit's. It made Karmik's app the contractual source of truth for money, which was convenient until the app's behaviour began to change for product reasons that had nothing to do with billing.

In 2022 Karmik acquired Hazri Systems, a small Pune company that made biometric attendance terminals, for ₹31 crore, mostly to serve clients whose sites had poor mobile coverage. The acquisition gave Karmik a second, independent record of attendance. The two systems were merged into a common warehouse table in 2023 by a pipeline that resolved conflicts with a rule nobody wrote down at the time: where an app punch and a device punch disagreed, the app punch won, because the app punch was what the contract referenced.

3. The industry around it

Indian frontline staffing in 2026 was a market of two halves. The organised incumbents — TeamLease, Quess Corp, Randstad India — ran large, relationship-led businesses with field supervisors and paper trails. The technology entrants, Karmik among them, competed on fill speed and on software, and recruited supply through job platforms like Apna and WorkIndia as well as directly. Demand had been transformed by quick commerce: dark-store networks operated by Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart had created hundreds of thousands of shift-based roles with volatile daily requirements, and festive peaks around Diwali and the Flipkart and Amazon sale events could double a city's requirement within a week.

Regulation was tightening and, importantly for Karmik, was tightening around definitions. The Code on Social Security had created a statutory category of gig and platform worker; Rajasthan and Karnataka had moved first on welfare boards funded by a cess on aggregator payouts, with other states drafting rules. Every one of those frameworks required an aggregator to report a count of workers and a value of payouts, and no two drafts defined the count identically. EPFO and ESIC contributions depended on days worked and wages paid. GST at eighteen per cent applied to manpower supply, which meant that a credit note was not merely a commercial gesture but a tax event with its own timing rules. Minimum wages varied by state, skill category and, in some states, by zone within the state.

Karmik's exposure ran beyond India. A two-person enterprise sales team in New Jersey sold to the Indian operations of United States-headquartered logistics firms. The Gulf pilot, run with Zubara Facilities Management in Dubai, placed Indian workers on UAE contracts where the labour regime, the working week and the meaning of a "deployed worker" were all different, and where Karmik billed in dirhams against a roster maintained by the client rather than by Karmik's app.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The sequence mattered, and Ira had reconstructed it only in the previous week.

In January 2025, Karmik introduced a quarterly incentive for the supply operations organisation based on "workers activated", defined as a registered worker who completed at least one shift in the quarter. The incentive was designed to attack a real problem: a large registered base that never worked.

Through 2025 the business grew quickly. In September, to reduce a rising volume of support tickets from workers who could not punch in — typically at large warehouse campuses where the gate and the work area were several hundred metres apart — the product team widened the geofence tolerance on the punch-in flow from 150 metres to 800 metres. The change shipped on 12 September. It was tested as a support-cost reduction, it worked, and support contacts fell 31 per cent. It was not reviewed by anyone who thought of the punch as a billing event, because the people who thought about billing were in finance and had never been shown a product change log.

In November, a deduplication job that merged worker records across mobile numbers began failing intermittently. It failed silently: the pipeline reported success because the job exited zero even when it processed no rows. The engineering manager in Pune found out in late January, when he was asked a different question.

In December, Tvarit began using a new warehouse-management system that logged which workers scanned into each store, and its operations team started comparing that log with Karmik's invoices. On 15 January it issued the notice. On 20 January the data science rebuild produced the 74,000 figure. On 2 February the auditors raised their query. On 6 February a prospective Series C investor asked for cohort-level retention data on active workers — the kind of request that could not be answered without picking a definition and standing behind it.

5. The people

Rajat Sinha, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Position: settle the Tvarit dispute quietly and commercially, do not restate the active-worker figure before the Series C closes, and treat the data science memo as an internal working paper. Incentive: the term sheet under negotiation values Karmik at about ₹2,400 crore and expires on 28 February. What he has not told the leadership team is that he quoted the 1.1 lakh figure to two investors in January, in writing.

Deepa Kamat, co-founder and chief technology officer, Bengaluru. Position: the pipeline is fixable, but not in eight days; the honest answer to Tvarit is that Karmik cannot presently prove either side of the dispute. Incentive: she owns the engineering roadmap and knows that a full reconciliation programme will consume most of a quarter. What she has not said is that she argued against the app-punch clause in 2021 and has kept the email.

Nithya Raghavan, chief financial officer, Bengaluru. Position: issue credit notes for the disputed amount, re-cut the revenue recognition policy and get ahead of the auditors. Incentive: she signs the accounts and the statutory filings, and a qualified audit opinion would be the end of the Series C in any case. What she has not said is that the auditors' query was triggered by a routine sample in which two of eight sampled shifts could not be evidenced at all.

Sanjay Dhar, vice-president of supply operations, based in Bengaluru but travelling constantly through Delhi NCR and Pune. Position: the app punches are genuine, Tvarit's store managers are reconstructing sign-off sheets from memory weeks later, and Karmik should defend its invoices. Incentive: his organisation's quarterly bonus is tied to workers activated and to fill rate, both of which fall under any stricter definition. What he has not said is that during the Diwali peak his field executives ran "assisted punch-in" camps at three large campuses, where a field executive helped workers punch in from a shared handset when workers' own phones had no charge or no data.

Dr Neha Kaul, head of data science, Toronto. Position: Karmik should adopt the rebuilt definition — a worker with at least one shift that is both punched and independently corroborated, deduplicated by bank account and PAN where available — and restate the last four quarters. Incentive: her credibility rests on the rebuild. What she has not said is that the rebuild could not obtain data for client-managed sites where only biometric terminals are used, roughly nine per cent of shifts, and that those workers are simply absent from her 74,000.

Vivek Athreya, engineering manager for the data platform, Pune. Position: the root cause is the 2023 merge rule that silently prefers app punches over device punches; he wants ten weeks to rebuild the attendance pipeline with an explicit, versioned conflict policy. Incentive: he has been asking for this work for two years. What he has not said is that he discovered the silent dedup failure on 28 January and has not yet quantified how many months it affected.

Farah Siddiqui, customer-success lead for APAC and the Gulf, Singapore. Position: pay the credit note, keep Tvarit, and move on. Incentive: her retention target covers the two largest accounts in the company. What she has not said is that Zubara in Dubai has asked for a reconciliation of its own, and that the Gulf roster is maintained by the client, so a Karmik-app-based defence would not even apply there.

Michael D'Souza, vice-president of enterprise sales, New Jersey. Position: whatever is decided must not reduce the published fill-rate figure, which appears in three live proposals. Incentive: his commission accelerator triggers on annual contract value booked before 31 March. What he has not said is that one of those proposals contains a service-level credit tied to fill rate as measured by Karmik's own system.

Lena Brandt, principal product designer, Berlin. Position: the geofence change was correct for workers and should not be reversed; the problem is that nobody told finance. Incentive: none material. What she has not said, because she was not asked, is that she raised the billing implication in a design review in August 2025 and was told it was out of scope.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

Rajat Sinha, leadership call, 21 January, 8.00 a.m. IST

"I am not saying the memo is wrong. I am saying that a memo written in three weeks by four people cannot overturn a number this company has reported for a year. Bring me the number that survives an audit, not the number that survives a rebuild."

Neha Kaul, reply on the same thread, 10.42 p.m. Toronto time

"Nothing in the rebuild is new analysis. It is the same shift table with one condition added: that something other than our own app agrees the shift happened. That condition removes a third of the base. If that is an unacceptable condition, I would like to understand which part of it we disagree with."

Sanjay Dhar, WhatsApp to Ira, 26 January

"Ira, please go to Bommasandra and stand at the gate at 5.45 a.m. The shifts are happening. We are being asked to prove attendance to a standard no staffing company in this country meets, by a client whose own sign-off sheets came in three weeks late through Diwali."

Vivek Athreya, engineering channel, 28 January, 11.50 p.m.

"Found it. The dedup job has been exiting zero with no rows processed since 14 November. Roughly two to four days a month, not contiguous. I can tell you it happened. I cannot yet tell you what it did to any number we published, because we overwrote the inputs."

Nithya Raghavan, email to the founders, 3 February

"The auditors sampled eight shifts. Six were evidenced. Two could not be evidenced from any system. I would rather we tell them what our policy is than have them tell us we do not have one."

Farah Siddiqui, Singapore, call notes, 5 February

"Zubara's contracts manager asked me, very politely, whether our India reconciliation would be extended to the Gulf roster. I said I would come back to him. Please note that in Dubai the roster is theirs, not ours, so none of the arguments we are preparing will work there."

Lena Brandt, Berlin, design review notes, 19 August 2025 (retrieved 6 February 2026)

"Flagging that widening the punch radius changes what a punch means for anyone downstream who treats it as evidence. Noted as out of scope for this review."

Michael D'Souza, New Jersey, sales forecast call, 6 February

"Understand the sensitivity. Just be aware that two of my three live proposals quote a 96 per cent fill rate measured on our system, and one of them attaches a service credit to it. If that number is restated I need to know before they countersign, not after."

8. The options as Ira sees them

Defend. Respond to Tvarit by 14 February citing the contract: attendance is evidenced by Karmik app punches, the punches exist, and the store-manager sign-off sheets are a weaker record produced late. Offer a goodwill credit of ₹1.2 crore covering the October and November outliers. This preserves revenue, protects Michael's proposals and does not disturb the Series C. It also requires Karmik to assert, in writing, that the app punch is reliable evidence — eight days after its own engineering manager reported that the identity pipeline had been failing silently, and five months after the punch's meaning was changed by a product release nobody logged.

Concede and restate. Issue credit notes for the full ₹6.82 crore, adopt the corroborated definition across all accounts, restate the active-worker figure to 74,300 and tell the investors before they ask. This is the version that is easiest to defend afterwards and costs the most now: ₹6.82 crore of cash of which ₹5.9 crore is already in workers' bank accounts, an EBITDA loss deepening to somewhere between ₹31 and ₹36 crore, and a headline metric falling by a third eleven days before a term sheet expires. It also concedes a standard of proof that no other client has yet asked for, to every other client at once.

Freeze and investigate. Ask Tvarit for a thirty-day standstill, commission Vivek's ten-week pipeline rebuild with an explicit and versioned conflict policy, hold the Series C to the next quarter, and publish nothing until the numbers can be reproduced. This is the answer most likely to produce a correct number and the one that spends the scarcest resource: Karmik has about eleven months of runway, Tvarit is under no obligation to grant a standstill, and a request for one is itself an admission.

Ira had written all three on a sheet of paper and had then written a fourth line underneath and left it unfinished. Every one of the three assumed that the task was to choose a number. But Tvarit needed a number that could be evidenced to a contract; the board needed a number that could be compared to last year; Karnataka needed a number computed on payouts; Zubara needed a number that Karmik's app never touched; and the supply operations team was being paid on a number that the same product change had inflated. She was not sure any single definition could serve all five, and she was not sure that saying so on Monday would be heard as clarity rather than as evasion.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The response to Tvarit was due 14 February, six days after Ira's Sunday night. The Series C term sheet expired on 28 February. The statutory audit had to be signed by 31 March, and a credit note issued after that date would fall into the following financial year with its own GST consequences. Karmik held about ₹186 crore of cash against a monthly burn of ₹17 crore. Tvarit represented 12.3 per cent of gross billings and its contract allowed termination on ninety days' notice. Vivek's rebuild required four engineers for ten weeks, drawn from the same team that was committed to the Gulf roster integration Farah had sold in November. Karnataka's cess filing was due in April on a basis Karmik had not yet chosen. And whatever Ira recommended, some 92,000 workers — or 74,000, or 1.1 lakh — would continue to arrive at warehouse gates at a quarter to six every morning, and would expect to be paid on Friday.

10. Questions for discussion

1. List every definition of a "worker" and of a "shift" that appears in this case, and identify for each the decision it exists to serve and the person, if any, who owns it.

2. Exhibit 2 shows the dispute widening from September. What are the three most plausible explanations, and what evidence in the case distinguishes between them? What evidence would you need that the case does not contain?

3. Exhibits 1, 4 and 5 each rest on data that a footnote qualifies. Which exhibit would most mislead a reader who skipped the footnotes, and in which direction?

4. Sanjay Dhar's assisted punch-in camps were a reasonable operational response to a real problem and also a corruption of a billing record. How should Karmik think about product changes that alter what an existing record means, and who should be in the room when such a change is approved?

5. Karmik must serve a client contract, a board, a prospective investor, two state regulators, an auditor and a Gulf client whose roster it does not control. Is a single canonical definition of attendance achievable here, and if not, what should Karmik build instead — and what does that cost?

6. What should Ira do on Monday morning, in what order, and with whom? What exactly would she say to the board on 12 February about the 1.1 lakh figure that the chief executive has already put in writing to two investors — and what would she do if she were told not to say it?

It was past one in the morning when Ira stopped writing. She had drafted the response to Tvarit three times. The first draft defended the invoices and she did not believe it. The second conceded them and she could not justify the ₹6.82 crore to a board that had approved a plan on different numbers. The third began by saying that Karmik could not at present determine which of its records was authoritative, and she had deleted it twice, because it was the only one that was true and she could not see how it ended.

She closed the laptop. On the table, the four printouts said 1,10,400, and 92,700, and 81,500, and 74,300, and every one of them had been produced by someone she trusted.
