Nirogi Care: Which Repeat Rate Is Real?

A ₹18 crore festive marketing budget rests on a single percentage that three teams compute three different ways.

1. Monday's number

At 7.15 on the evening of Thursday, 6 November 2025, Shalini Iyer was the last person on the fourth floor of Nirogi Care's office in Madhapur, Hyderabad. As director of product for the consumer app, she had four working days to settle a question that had been politely avoided for a year. On Monday morning the leadership team would lock the marketing budget for the January quarter, and the case for raising it from ₹9 crore to ₹18 crore rested on one figure: the repeat rate of newly acquired customers.

The growth team's deck said 46 per cent. The finance team's monthly pack said 31 per cent. The operations dashboard, which the warehouse and delivery teams watched, said 38 per cent. All three had been produced that week, from the same underlying orders, by competent people who could each show their query. Shalini's own view was that the difference of fifteen percentage points was worth roughly ₹9 crore of spend and, if the lower figure was right, about eight months of cash.

2. Nirogi Care

Nirogi Care was founded in 2019 by two pharmacists and a former Infosys engineer, and sold prescription medicines, over-the-counter products and at-home diagnostic tests through an app and a network of 41 fulfilment centres across eleven states. By October 2025 it served about 3.1 million customers a year at an annualised gross merchandise value of ₹640 crore, with roughly 58 per cent of revenue from chronic-medicine refills — diabetes, hypertension, thyroid — and the remainder split between acute prescriptions, OTC and diagnostics.

It was a crowded market. Tata 1mg, Apollo 24|7, PharmEasy and Netmeds held the large share positions; Reliance Retail's Netmeds and Amazon Pharmacy pressed on price; and in the previous eighteen months Zepto and Swiggy Instamart had begun delivering OTC products in ten minutes in the metros, which had pulled Nirogi Care's convenience-led customers away while leaving its chronic base largely intact. Payments ran over UPI through Razorpay; prescriptions were validated against state drug-licensing rules; and the DPDP Act had recently tightened how long Nirogi Care could retain identifiable health-order history, which mattered more to this story than anyone expected.

The team was distributed by accident rather than design. Engineering sat in Bengaluru and Pune, the design lead worked from Berlin, the senior data scientist was in Toronto, the customer-success lead for corporate accounts was in Singapore, and a two-person enterprise sales team in New Jersey sold employee-health benefits to Indian-founded firms in the United States. The largest of those corporate accounts was a construction group in Dubai that bought medicine benefits for 4,200 Indian employees and their families.

3. How three numbers came to exist

The growth team had built its repeat-rate dashboard in 2023, when Nirogi Care was small enough that nobody questioned it. It defined a repeat customer as anyone who had placed a second order, of any kind, at any time after the first. It counted orders at the shipment level, so a basket split between the Hyderabad and Chennai warehouses counted as two. It counted diagnostics bookings and pharmacy orders together. And it identified customers by app account, of which a single household frequently had several.

Finance had built its own definition in 2024, for the investor pack. A repeat customer was one who had taken delivery of a second order, paid for and not returned, within ninety days of the first, with accounts deduplicated by mobile number. Operations sat in between: delivered orders, deduplicated by address, any time window, shipments merged.

Ishaan Mehra, the data scientist in Toronto, had flagged the problem twice in 2024. Both times the thread died because it arrived in the Hyderabad morning after the meeting it concerned. In September, Sneha Kulkarni's engineering team in Pune had shipped an order-splitting change that improved delivery times for multi-item baskets; nobody connected it to the fact that the growth team's repeat rate rose four points in October.

4. The people

Karthik Reddy, vice-president of growth, Hyderabad, had built the ₹18 crore case and believed it. His performance-marketing channels were showing a blended customer acquisition cost of ₹740, and at a 46 per cent repeat rate the cohort paid back inside five months. He had held back spend through two quarters and watched Tata 1mg and Apollo 24|7 take share in Pune and Ahmedabad. He wanted a decision, not a review.

Nandini Pillai, financial controller, had joined eighteen months earlier from a listed retailer and had introduced the ninety-day delivered definition precisely because the board had once been shown a growth number that could not be tied to the ledger. She was not opposed to spending; she was opposed to spending against a number nobody owned.

Ishaan Mehra, senior data scientist in Toronto, thought all three definitions were defensible and none of them answered the question being asked. His own analysis showed that repeat behaviour differed so sharply between chronic-refill customers and OTC customers that a single blended rate was misleading regardless of definition.

Wen Li Tan, customer-success lead in Singapore, had a narrower but sharper interest. The Dubai construction group's contract was priced on "active beneficiaries", and she had been quoting the growth team's account-level figures in renewal reviews. If the definition changed, she would have to explain to a client why the number she had reported all year was going to fall.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. Bridge from the growth repeat rate to the finance repeat rate, August 2025 acquisition cohort (base: 214,000 first-time customers)
LineRule that explains itRepeat rate
Growth dashboardSecond order placed, any type, any time, app account46.0%
Less split shipments counted twiceOne basket, two warehouses, two order rows(3.9)
Less orders placed but never deliveredCancelled, prescription rejected, payment failed(4.1)
Less returns and refundsDelivered then returned within the window(1.3)
Less duplicate accounts in one householdDeduplicated by mobile number(2.2)
Less second orders after day 90Finance measures a 90-day window(3.5)
Finance monthly packDelivered, paid, retained, within 90 days31.0%

Note: the operations figure of 38.0 per cent is the same bridge stopped after the third line. Household deduplication is an estimate; DPDP retention limits removed some historical mobile numbers, so the true adjustment may be 0.3 to 0.5 points larger.

Exhibit 1 was the first thing Shalini asked for, and it took Ishaan a day and a half. Every line is a rule rather than a rounding, which is why the three numbers stopped being a dispute and became an explanation. Two lines deserve particular attention: the 3.9 points from split shipments are pure artefact, created by a September engineering change, and the 4.1 points of undelivered orders are partly real demand that Nirogi Care failed to serve.

Exhibit 2. Unit economics of the ₹18 crore plan under each definition (blended CAC ₹740; contribution margin ₹128 per delivered order)
Definition usedRepeat rateDelivered orders per new customer, 90 daysContribution, 90 daysMonths to CAC payback
Growth (placed, any time)46.0%2.4₹3074.8
Operations (delivered, any time)38.0%1.9₹2436.7
Finance (delivered, 90 days)31.0%1.6₹2059.4

Note: contribution margin excludes fixed fulfilment overhead and the ₹44 per order last-mile subsidy currently running in Tier-2 cities.

Exhibit 2 converts the definitional argument into money. Nirogi Care's board had approved an investment case on the understanding that new cohorts pay back within six months. Under the growth definition the plan clears that bar comfortably; under the finance definition it misses it by more than three months, which on ₹18 crore of spend is roughly ₹5.6 crore of cash tied up longer than the plan assumes.

Exhibit 3 is the one that unsettled Shalini most. Chronic-refill customers repeat at 58 per cent even on the strictest definition, and OTC-only customers at 12 per cent. Since roughly 62 per cent of the incremental ₹9 crore was earmarked for broad-reach performance channels that historically delivered OTC and diagnostics buyers, the plan would spend most of the new money on the segments where every definition agreed that repeat behaviour was weak.

6. The options

Option A: lock the ₹18 crore now, reconcile later. The festive and New Year window is the strongest acquisition period of the year, and competitors are spending. Karthik's channels can absorb the money within a fortnight. The cost is that Nirogi Care commits ₹9 crore of incremental spend against a payback assumption that Exhibit 2 suggests may be wrong by three to five months, and the definitional problem survives to cause the same argument at the next budget.

Option B: hold at ₹9 crore and fix the definitions first. Two weeks of work would produce one owned, versioned definition of a repeat customer, a restated history, and a metric registry entry. The cost is the window: a fortnight of the quarter's best demand, plausibly 30,000 to 40,000 customers, conceded to competitors, and a growth team that will read the decision as a vote of no confidence.

Option C: approve a restricted tranche with a named owner and a gate. Release ₹12 crore now, but restrict the incremental ₹3 crore to channels and creatives that acquire chronic-refill customers, where all three definitions agree the economics work. Simultaneously appoint an owner for the repeat-rate definition, publish it as version 1 with the Exhibit 1 bridge attached, and set a checkpoint on day 21 at which the remaining ₹6 crore is released or withheld on the basis of the agreed metric. The cost is complexity and a growth team operating with less money than it asked for, plus the risk that a 21-day read is too short for a 90-day metric.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Walk through Exhibit 1. Which of the six bridge lines represent genuine differences of business question, and which represent defects that should simply be fixed?

2. Who should own the definition of "repeat customer" at Nirogi Care — growth, finance, product or the data team — and what exactly does ownership entitle that person to decide?

3. Exhibit 3 suggests the blended repeat rate may be the wrong object of the argument. How should that change the budget question, if at all?

4. What should Shalini recommend on Monday, and what would she say to Karthik and to Wen Li Tan about the numbers each of them has already reported?

8. A note for the learner

The lens for this case is that a metric is not a number but a definition with an owner, a version and a decision it serves. Once that is accepted, the fifteen-point gap stops being a credibility contest between two teams and becomes a bridge: six rules, each of which can be inspected and each of which belongs to somebody. Note that the bridge does more than settle the argument. It separates the three points of pure artefact created by a shipping change from the four points of genuinely lost demand, and only the second of those is a product problem worth a roadmap slot.

A well-reasoned answer will do three things. It will name a single definition for company-wide use and justify the choice by the decision it informs — a cash-payback decision argues for the delivered, time-bounded, deduplicated definition, because that is the population that actually generates the contribution margin in the model. It will preserve rather than delete the other measurements, renaming them so that growth keeps the funnel diagnostic it needs and customer success keeps a beneficiary count it can explain to Dubai. And it will assign an owner with the authority to refuse changes, along with a version number and a restatement note covering the September order-splitting artefact.

One defensible path is Option C. It respects the deadline rather than pretending the festive window can be recovered later, it spends the incremental money where the evidence is strongest under every definition rather than where it is strongest under only one, and it forces the definitional work to happen under real pressure, which is when such work actually gets done. The day-21 gate should be read honestly: at that point the 90-day metric will not have matured, so the gate must be set on a leading indicator that the owner has defined in advance — second delivered order within 21 days, say — with the explicit acknowledgement that it is a proxy and with the full cohort read scheduled for February. The weakness of the path is real and should be stated in the recommendation rather than hidden: it asks the organisation to do two hard things at once, and if the definitional work slips, Nirogi Care will have spent ₹12 crore against a number it still cannot defend.
